title: Bollywood Had Its Worst May in Five Years. Tamil, Malayalam, and Marathi Cinema Didn't Notice.
excerpt: Karuppu crossed ₹253 crore. Drishyam 3 hit ₹170 crore. Raja Shivaji became the highest-grossing Marathi film ever. Bollywood's two big May releases combined for less than Drishyam 3's overseas gross alone.
body:
May 2026 was supposed to be Bollywood's month to breathe. After the Dhurandhar 2 juggernaut swallowed the first quarter and Border 2 took its share in April, the Hindi film industry had two mid-budget releases lined up for May — Pati Patni Aur Woh Do and Chand Mera Dil — with clear open corridors and no competition from tentpoles. The plan was simple: fill the gap, collect the spoils, move on.

Instead, both films tanked. And while Bollywood was busy underperforming, three other film industries were having the month of their lives.

## The Numbers Tell the Story

Here is what the May 2026 Indian box office looks like as of May 26:

| Film | Industry | India Gross | Worldwide Gross |
|------|----------|------------|-----------------|
| **Karuppu** | Tamil | ₹184.25 Cr | ₹253.25 Cr |
| **Drishyam 3** | Malayalam | ₹79.65 Cr | ₹170.25 Cr |
| **Raja Shivaji** | Marathi | ₹109.80 Cr | ₹114.00 Cr |
| **Deool Band 2** | Marathi | ₹26.50 Cr | ₹26.50 Cr |
| **Pati Patni Aur Woh Do** | Hindi | ₹46.30 Cr | ₹53.85 Cr |
| **Chand Mera Dil** | Hindi | ~₹18 Cr | ~₹21 Cr |

Read that again. Bollywood's two May releases — combined — grossed about ₹75 crore worldwide. Drishyam 3's overseas gross alone is ₹90 crore. A Malayalam film's international audience outspent all of Hindi cinema's domestic May output.

## Suriya's Karuppu: The Tamil Blockbuster Nobody Predicted

Suriya had not delivered a clean hit in years. His previous films had underperformed against expectations, and there was genuine scepticism about whether his star power had eroded permanently. Then RJ Balaji directed him in Karuppu — a film about a temple guardian deity who discovers systemic corruption in his village and takes the fight to court, not to the battlefield — and the audience showed up.

₹253 crore worldwide in 12 days. More than double Suriya's previous biggest grosser, Singam 2. Tamil Nadu alone contributed over ₹120 crore gross. The overseas performance was equally dominant, with strong runs in the United States, the UK, and the Gulf.

For NRI audiences, Karuppu landed differently. Here was a Tamil film that played in multiplexes across North America alongside Hollywood blockbusters and held its own. The AMC in Fremont and the Regal in Edison were running it in prime slots. That used to be reserved for Shah Rukh Khan vehicles.

## Drishyam 3: The Franchise That Prints Money Abroad

Mohanlal's Drishyam 3 arrived with mixed reviews and unstoppable momentum. The franchise's brand is so strong that it front-loaded ₹90 crore overseas in six days — making it the kind of international performer that most Hindi films can only dream about.

Kerala remains the engine, contributing ₹50 crore gross in six days. But it is the overseas story that matters for the diaspora. North America crossed $1.64 million. Australia cleared A$850K. New Zealand, a market barely anyone tracks, added NZ$240K. Malayalam cinema has built an international infrastructure — organised fan groups, pre-booked theatre chains, dedicated screening clusters in NRI-heavy metro areas — that now rivals what Bollywood spent decades constructing.

## Marathi Cinema's Impossible Double

Perhaps the most remarkable story of May belongs to Marathi cinema. Riteish Deshmukh's Raja Shivaji, released on May 1, crossed ₹110 crore to become the highest-grossing Marathi film of all time, breaking Sairat's decade-old record. Then, three weeks later, Pravin Tarde's devotional drama Deool Band 2 opened to ₹2.45 crore — modest by any standard — and word of mouth turned it into a phenomenon. In six days, it has grossed ₹26.50 crore and is marching towards ₹50 crore.

Two blockbusters in the same month from an industry that, ten years ago, was happy to produce one per year. The Pune and Mumbai Marathi-speaking audience has found its theatrical legs, and the implications extend to the diaspora: Marathi films are increasingly showing up in US and UK theatres, screening to packed NRI audiences who never had access to them before.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

The practical shift is already visible in NRI movie-going habits. Five years ago, the default Friday night Indian movie was a Hindi film. Today, NRI audiences in the Bay Area, New Jersey, and London are choosing between a Tamil blockbuster, a Malayalam thriller, and a Marathi historical epic on the same weekend.

Theatre chains have noticed. BookMyShow's international arm now tracks pre-sales for South Indian and regional films with the same granularity it once reserved for Bollywood. Distributors like Phars Film Co and UFO Moviez are expanding their non-Hindi slates aggressively.

The linguistic diversity of the Indian box office is no longer a trade publication curiosity. It is how people watch movies now — in India and everywhere Indians live.

Bollywood will be fine. Dhurandhar 2 is still running in its ninth week. The pipeline for the rest of 2026 includes Peddi, Alpha, Ramayana, and Mahavatar. But May 2026 offered the clearest proof yet that the Indian film industry's centre of gravity has permanently shifted. The question is no longer whether regional cinema can compete with Bollywood. It is whether Bollywood can compete with regional cinema.

*Sources: Sacnilk, Pinkvilla, Koimoi, BookMyShow*
